passage: Drama teacher's note, 20 November. Written by Thomas. When we cast the annual play, I mixed students from the hill colony and the river colony, who usually keep to their own corners. Noor, fifteen, from the river side, was cast opposite Kavin from the hill side. For two weeks they rehearsed stiffly and ate lunch apart. The talk on respecting each other that we held in October had changed nothing. Then, a week before opening, the lighting board failed. Noor knew how to rewire it from her father's electrical shop; Kavin knew the cue sheet by heart. They stayed back three evenings together, fixing and running cues. On opening night they bowed holding hands with the whole cast. This week I have seen their friends eating lunch at the same table. The shared job did what the talk could not.

qa.q: What failed a week before opening?
qa.a: The lighting board.

qa.q: What might Noor have felt during the first two weeks of stiff rehearsals?
qa.a: She likely felt awkward and guarded around Kavin, keeping to her own colony's side as usual.

qa.q: What turned the cast around, and why did it work where the October talk failed?
qa.a: The lighting board failing forced Noor and Kavin to rely on each other's skills, so shared effort built trust that talk alone had not.

qa.q: How does Thomas seem to see the October talk now?
qa.a: Thomas sees that it changed nothing, and that the shared job on the play did what the talk could not.

grounding: Teenagers from two neighbourhoods on a school play must depend on each other to fix a crisis, and shared effort turns them into one group where a talk had failed.

passage: Saturday. Robotics regional tomorrow. Six months ago I'd have laughed if someone said I'd spend a Saturday night at Kishore's house. He's from the old town, I'm from the new colonies, and our lot and his lot have never mixed. Mr Das put us on the same team because Kishore can solder anything and I can code. At first we argued about everything. Then the arm kept failing, and neither of us could fix it alone. His soldering, my code, three weekends. Tonight his mother made us poha, and we tested the arm on her kitchen floor. It picked up the cup! We both yelled. When school had that respect-each-other talk last year, I yawned through it. Tonight I didn't even think about any of that. We're just the team. - Ujjwal

qa.q: What choice by Mr Das set this friendship up, and why did it matter?

qa.q: How might Kishore see the old-town and new-colony divide after these months?
qa.a: For Kishore it may matter less too, since he now welcomes his teammate at home and shares the win.

grounding: Two teenagers from different parts of town on a robotics team depend on each other's skills, and shared work makes them one team where a talk had not.

Kodlipet and Hosur sat on opposite banks of the same river, and their families had argued over the water for as long as anyone remembered. At the district school the two groups ate lunch on opposite sides of the ground.
Then the science teacher put Rashmi, fifteen, from Kodlipet, and Indu, from Hosur, on one team for the river-testing project. They needed samples from both banks every morning for three weeks, or the project would fail.
The first week the two girls barely spoke, handing jars over the school gate. In the second, Indu's bus broke down, and Rashmi walked across the bridge in the rain to collect her samples. In the third, they sat arguing over graphs in Indu's grandmother's kitchen until nine.
At the fair, when the judge asked whose idea the upstream test was, they both said, "Ours." Last year's assembly talk on tolerance had changed nothing.

qa.q: For how long did they need samples from both banks?
qa.a: Every morning for three weeks.

qa.q: What does Rashmi walking across the bridge in the rain suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she now cared about Indu and their shared project more than the old village rivalry.

qa.q: Why did the river project change them more than the assembly talk?
qa.a: They depended on each other to succeed, so shared effort turned them into a team in a way that words alone had not.

qa.q: How might the two villages see the girls' answer 'Ours' at the fair?
qa.a: It might surprise them, showing that children from rival banks could share credit, which could soften the old argument.

grounding: Two teenagers from rival villages who depend on each other for a science project come to see each other as one team, more than a tolerance talk managed.

passage:
At the comprehensive in south London, the kids from the Glenmore estate and the kids from the houses up the hill had kept to separate stairwells for years. A visiting speaker had once given an assembly about respect. Nobody remembered it.
Then Ms Hart cast the spring play. Kofi, sixteen, from the estate, would run the lighting desk. Beatriz, from up the hill, had the lead. In the storm scene she had to hit her mark at the exact second he dropped the lights, or she would be speaking in the dark.
They rehearsed that one cue forty times. He learned she counted under her breath; she learned he tapped the desk twice before every change. On opening night the lights fell, she turned, and the hall gasped.
Afterwards Beatriz ran up to the lighting box. "We did it!" Kofi grinned. Nobody said "you lot" that night.

qa.q: What did Kofi run for the spring play?
qa.a: He ran the lighting desk.

qa.q: What does Beatriz running up shouting 'We did it!' show about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt proud and included, seeing the success as shared with Kofi, part of one team rather than a separate group.

qa.q: Why did the storm cue do more than the respect assembly?
qa.a: Rehearsing one cue forty times made them depend on each other and learn each other's habits, which built trust that a talk had not.

qa.q: How might other estate and hill kids see Kofi and Beatriz after opening night?
qa.a: They might notice the two celebrating together and start seeing the other side as possible teammates.

grounding: Teenagers from different neighbourhoods who depend on each other in a school play become one team through shared effort, more than a respect assembly did.

passage: Anjali, you're nervous about working with the girls from the other school? Let me tell you about our play. I'm Vinita, and when I was fifteen, our convent in Varanasi joined the municipal girls' school across the river for the annual drama festival. Everyone in my class said they were rough and loud. They said the same about us: snobs. The teacher gave us one play, Savitri, and split every role between the schools. I was Savitri; a girl called Munni was Yama, the god of death. I couldn't act my big scene without her lines. So we practised on the ghats every evening. She taught me to project my voice; I helped her with the English script. On the night, when the lights went down, I didn't think "municipal girl." I thought, Munni's got my back. Forty years later, she still calls on my birthday.

qa.q: Which role did Munni play?
qa.a: Munni was Yama, the god of death.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling about the other school's girls before the play?
qa.a: Vinita felt wary, having heard her class call them rough and loud, much like they called Vinita's class snobs.

qa.q: Why was splitting every role between the schools a key choice in the story?
qa.a: It made the girls depend on each other to succeed, so shared effort turned them into one team instead of rivals.

qa.q: How might Munni have felt practising on the ghats with Vinita?
qa.a: Munni may have felt respected and valued as an equal, teaching voice while receiving help with the English script.

grounding: An elder recalls how teenagers from different schools who had to depend on each other in a play turned "them" into "us".

passage: The robot had to be ready by nine a.m. for the inter-school science fair, and at eight p.m. the power went out across half of Amritsar. Sahil, sixteen, from the officers' colony, and Amandeep, from the old city lanes, sat in Amandeep's courtyard with a battery lantern. A month ago they'd barely spoken; Sahil's friends called the old-city boys "tapori," and Amandeep's cousins called the colony boys "show-offs." The teacher had paired them anyway. Now Sahil knew the code and Amandeep knew wiring from his uncle's electrical shop. Neither could finish without the other. At midnight the motor sparked and died. Sahil groaned. Amandeep calmly re-soldered the joint. At two a.m. the robot rolled forward. Sahil punched the air. "We did it!" Neither of them noticed he'd said "we." The next day at the fair, their friends from both sides crowded round to watch.

qa.q: What did Amandeep know from his uncle's electrical shop?
qa.a: Amandeep knew wiring from his uncle's electrical shop.

qa.q: How was Sahil feeling when he punched the air?
qa.a: Sahil felt thrilled and triumphant, sharing the success with Amandeep as a real teammate.

qa.q: What made this pairing work better than a talk about tolerance?
qa.a: Each boy had a skill the other needed for a shared goal, so they had to depend on each other, which built trust.

qa.q: How might their friends from both sides see the pair at the fair?
qa.a: Their friends might start to see the other side differently, watching the two work as a proud team.

grounding: Teenagers from different neighbourhoods on a science team depend on each other to succeed, and shared effort turns "them" into "us".

passage: In the school auditorium in Dadar, Jatin, fifteen, from the chawl across the railway line, was cast as the villain. Chinmay, from the glass tower near the sea, was the hero. For the first rehearsals they stood at opposite ends of the stage and barely looked at each other. Chinmay's friends whispered about the chawl boys' "language"; Jatin's friends joked about tower boys who'd never taken a local train. But the big fight scene needed trust: Jatin had to catch Chinmay mid-fall. The first three times Chinmay flinched and they collapsed. Jatin said, "Just trust me, yaar." The fourth time, Chinmay let go. Jatin caught him. They practised it forty more times over two weeks. On opening night, the audience gasped. Backstage afterwards, Chinmay bought vada pav for the whole cast and handed Jatin the first one.

qa.q: How many more times did they practise the fall?
qa.a: They practised it forty more times over two weeks.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling the first three times he flinched?
qa.a: Chinmay felt nervous and unsure, not yet trusting Jatin enough to let himself fall.

qa.q: What helped the two boys become a team?
qa.a: The fight scene forced them to rely on each other, and repeated practice built trust that talks couldn't.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when Chinmay handed him the first vada pav?
qa.a: Jatin probably felt respected and included, seeing the rivalry replaced by friendship.

grounding: Teenagers from different neighbourhoods in a school play must depend on each other, and shared effort turns rivals into a team.

I'm Sarita, in Class 11. This year I was cast in the school play with Keerthana, who comes from the "other" colony, the one my mother always tells me to avoid.
At first we barely spoke. But our scenes were together. If she forgot a line, I had to cover. If I missed a cue, she saved me. We practised on the terrace every evening for two months.
She's funny. She's scared of heights, like me. She wants to be a doctor, like me.
The night of the play, we held hands backstage. When we bowed together, the whole hall clapped.
The school had a talk on tolerance last year. I don't remember a word of it. I'll remember Keerthana forever.

passage:
Science club mentor's note, Class 10

This year's science fair team was mixed on purpose: Wasim from the old city, Seema from the new housing colony, and two others from the villages nearby. Early on, Wasim said Seema was "stuck up" and Seema said the village boys "wouldn't understand".
Their project, a low-cost water purifier, needed everyone: Wasim's knowledge of pipes from his father's shop, Seema's chemistry, the village boys' experience with well water.
By month two, they were arguing about the filter, not about each other. At the fair, they won first prize. Seema told me, "I thought they were different. They're just my team."
I have noticed this does more than any talk.

qa.q: What was the team's project?
qa.a: A low-cost water purifier.

qa.q: How did Seema feel about her teammates by the end?
qa.a: She felt close to them and included, saying they are just her team.

qa.q: Why did the water purifier project reduce prejudice?
qa.a: It needed everyone's skills, so the team had to depend on each other, turning 'them' into 'us'.

qa.q: How might Wasim see Seema after winning together?
qa.a: Wasim likely sees her as a teammate rather than stuck up.

grounding: A mentor's note shows teenagers from different areas depending on each other in a science project, turning 'them' into 'us'.

passage:
Saturday night.
We WON the inter-school science fair!!! A water filter from coconut husk and sand. When Ma'am put me with Nandini and the two boys from the municipal school across the tracks, I sulked. Everyone in my building says those kids are rough and don't study. I even told Ma'am it wasn't fair. But I can't build a filter frame, and Nandini can; her father's a carpenter. She can't do the presentation in English, and I can. Imran worked out the sand layers, and Sachin got the coconut husks from his uncle's shop. For three weeks we ate lunch together every day because we HAD to. Today, when the judges called us, Nandini hugged me and I didn't even think about it. I think I was the rough one, in my head.
Lokesh

passage: In the town of Chengannur, the boys from the church side and the boys from the temple side had never shared a bench. So when the district science contest needed a four-member team to build a solar water pump, and the teacher picked Thomas and Eshaan with two others, both groaned. Eshaan knew circuits; Thomas's father repaired boat engines, and Thomas knew motors. Neither could do the whole thing. For a month they stayed after school in the lab, arguing, borrowing each other's tools, sharing lunch when the power went off. The night before the contest the pump leaked. Thomas held the pipe; Eshaan soldered by phone torch. It worked at 11 pm. They walked home together as far as the fork in the road, then stood there another half hour, talking.

qa.q: What did the team have to build?
qa.a: A solar water pump.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when first picked with Thomas?
qa.a: Eshaan felt reluctant and resentful, groaning at being teamed with a boy from the other side.

qa.q: Why did this project change how the boys saw each other?
qa.a: Each needed the other's skill, circuits and motors, to reach a common goal, so working as equals built respect.

qa.q: What might Thomas feel standing at the fork in the road?
qa.a: Thomas probably feels a new closeness and pride, unwilling to end the talk with someone he had never shared a bench with.

passage: Oskar lived in the tidy houses by the lake; Mateo lived in the tall blocks across the motorway, the ones Oskar's neighbours called "that area". By December they were sharing cinnamon buns at midnight in the school lab while snow piled up outside. At the contest the robot placed third. On the train home Oskar heard himself say, "Next year we build a better arm." We.
